A handicap is anything that puts you at a disadvantage — something that makes it harder for you to do something, succeed at something, or compete fairly against others.

Think of it this way: imagine two people racing. One is wearing heavy boots, and the other is wearing light sneakers. The heavy boots are a handicap — they don't stop the person from running, but they make success much harder than it would otherwise be.

A handicap is almost always relative. It is a disadvantage compared to others or compared to what would normally be expected. Something is only a handicap if it puts you behind where you could or should be.
The Two Main Worlds of This Word

The word "handicap" lives in two very different worlds — everyday life, and the world of sports. It means something slightly different in each, so let's look at both carefully.

1. In Everyday Life — A Disadvantage or Obstacle

In general, everyday use, a handicap is any condition, circumstance, or limitation that holds someone back or makes their path harder than someone else's.

This can be:

  • A physical limitation — e.g., if a pianist has an injured hand, that injury is a handicap in their career.
  • A circumstantial disadvantage — e.g., growing up in poverty can be a handicap when competing for opportunities in life.
  • A knowledge or skill gap — e.g., not speaking the local language is a handicap when you move to a new country.
  • A resource disadvantage — e.g., a small company with a tiny budget faces a handicap when competing against large corporations.

Notice that a handicap doesn't make something impossible — it just makes it harder. It tips the scales against you.

A few clear examples:

  • "His lack of formal education was a significant handicap in his job search."
  • "The team's star player being injured was a serious handicap going into the championship."
  • "Being colour-blind is a handicap for someone who wants to become a pilot."

2. In Sports — A Deliberate System to Make Competition Fair

This is where the word gets a very specific and technical meaning. In sports, a handicap is an artificial disadvantage given to a stronger competitor (or an artificial advantage given to a weaker one) so that everyone has a roughly equal chance of winning.

Why would you do this? Because sports are more fun and more fair when the outcome isn't already obvious. If a champion golfer plays against a beginner, the beginner has no real chance — the game is pointless. A handicap system fixes this.

The most famous example is golf:

Golf Handicap

In golf, your handicap is a number that represents how many strokes above (or below) the "perfect" score you typically play. A beginner might have a handicap of 28, while an expert might have a handicap of 2.

When they compete against each other:

  • The beginner gets to subtract their handicap strokes from their final score.
  • This effectively gives the beginner a head start to compensate for their lower skill level.
  • The result? Both players are now competing on a level playing field.

So in golf, a higher handicap = less skilled player (because they need more strokes taken off to level things up), and a lower handicap = more skilled player.

In everyday language, this logic carries over — you'll often hear people say someone has a "low handicap" as a compliment (meaning they're highly skilled), or a "high handicap" to mean they're still developing.

Horse Racing Handicap

In horse racing, a handicap race is one where stronger, faster horses are made to carry extra weight during the race. The extra weight slows them down just enough to give slower horses a better chance. Here, the "handicap" is the burden imposed on the stronger competitor.
An Important Third Usage — Disability (Now Largely Outdated)

Historically, "handicap" was widely used as a noun to refer to a physical or mental disability. For example, people used to say "He has a physical handicap" to mean he has a disability.

You will still come across this usage in older books, films, and documents, so you need to know it exists. However, this usage is now largely considered outdated and insensitive by most style guides and disability communities. The preferred word today is "disability" — not "handicap."

Why the shift? Because the word "handicap" carries connotations of being "held back" or "lessened," which many people with disabilities rightfully find reductive and inaccurate. A disability is a characteristic, not automatically a disadvantage in all areas of life.

So in modern writing and speech, avoid using "handicap" to refer to a person's disability.
The Unifying Thread Across All Meanings

No matter which context you're in, every use of "handicap" shares one common thread:

A handicap is something that creates an unequal condition — either naturally (a disadvantage someone faces) or deliberately (a balancing mechanism imposed by a sport's rules) — that affects someone's ability to perform, compete, or succeed on equal terms.

When it's natural (everyday life), a handicap is generally unwanted — it's a challenge to overcome.
When it's deliberate (sports), a handicap is designed and purposeful — it's a tool to create fairness.

ContextWhat "handicap" means
  • Everyday life: A disadvantage or obstacle that holds someone back compared to others.
  • Golf: A numerical score adjustment that levels the playing field between players of different abilities.
  • Horse racing: Extra weight assigned to a stronger horse to slow it down and make competition fairer.
  • Historical (now outdated): A physical or mental disability — avoid this usage today; use "disability" instead.

The word is always about imbalance — and either suffering from it, or correcting it.
